entries.topic: Bible institutes, Moody Bible Institute, Dallas Theological Seminary as institutional carriers of dispensationalism

claims.text: Moody Bible Institute was founded in Chicago in 1886 by the evangelist Dwight L. Moody (as the Chicago Evangelization Society) and took Moody's name after his death in 1899; its publishing arm began in 1894 as the Bible Institute Colportage Association (Moody Press from 1941); its station WMBI began in 1926, described as the first non-commercial Christian radio station in America; the Moody network owns 36 stations and supplies programming to more than 700 outlets; 2,341 students (2025); described as dispensational.

Christianity Today (Olsen, 1961): Nyack (1882) and Moody (1886) were the first Bible institutes; 'More than 200 Bible institutes and colleges are presently in existence'; the schools proclaimed among core beliefs 'the imminent return of Jesus Christ'.

Dallas Theological Seminary was founded in 1924 as the Evangelical Theological College by Lewis Sperry Chafer, his brother Rollin T. Chafer and W.H. Griffith Thomas (who died before classes began); known for popularizing dispensationalism; premillennial, dispensational, inerrantist, non-denominational; 1,377 FTE students (2025); over 15,000 alumni in 97 countries (2014); alumni include David Jeremiah, Andy Stanley, Tony Evans, Chuck Swindoll.

DTS's own history: the seminary 'opened its doors in 1924' with 13 students; first graduating class 1927; 'more than 16,000 DTS alumni'; about 2,600 current students; programmes in Arabic, Chinese and Spanish.

DTS Hendricks Center podcast (8 Oct 2024): Craig Blaising describes dispensationalism as keeping Israel and the church distinct; 'Israel stays in the plan of God all the way to the end'; the tradition includes 'progressive' and 'traditional' versions.

Hal Lindsey graduated from Dallas Theological Seminary in 1962 with a Master of Theology; worked with Campus Crusade for Christ until 1969; held that 'the establishment of the State of Israel in May 1948 is the fulfillment of this major prophecy'; died 25 November 2024 in Tulsa aged 95.

entries.topic: Spread abroad: Latin America (Guatemala, Honduras, Paraguay, Brazil) and Africa (Nigeria); embassy decisions vs material interests

claims.text: Pew 2014 (fieldwork Oct 2013-Feb 2014; 30,000+ interviews in 18 countries and Puerto Rico): Protestants 41% of adults in Guatemala (Catholic 50%), 41% in Honduras (46%), 26% in Brazil (61%), 7% in Paraguay (89%); region 19% Protestant, 69% Catholic; sample 1,500 Guatemala, 2,000 Brazil.

Pew 2014 as reported by CT: about 2 in 3 Protestants region-wide identify as Pentecostal or attend a Pentecostal church; only 23% of Guatemalan and 26% of Honduran Protestants were raised Catholic, vs 68% in Paraguay.
Brazil census 2022 (IBGE, released June 2025): evangelicals 26.9% (47.4 million), up from 21.6% in 2010; Catholics 56.7% (100.2 million), down from 65.1%.

Guatemala opened its embassy in Jerusalem on 16 May 2018, two days after the US; Netanyahu and President Jimmy Morales, 'an evangelical', cut the ribbon; Morales: 'a step forward in favour of union and friendship'; Guatemala's UN ambassador Jorge Garcia Granados was 'one of the architects' of the 1947 partition plan; Paraguay planned to move by month's end.

Paraguay moved its embassy to Jerusalem in 2018 under Horacio Cartes; Mario Abdo Benitez reversed it months later and Israel temporarily closed its embassy in Asuncion; President Santiago Pena reopened it on 12 December 2024; embassies in Jerusalem: US, Guatemala, Honduras, Kosovo, Papua New Guinea; AP notes Guatemala and Honduras have 'similarly strong evangelical churches'.

Brazil: Bolsonaro suggested in January 2019 Brazil would follow the US; on 31 March 2019 during his Israel visit Brazil announced an office in Jerusalem 'to promote trade, investment, technology and innovation' as part of its Tel Aviv embassy; Vice-President Hamilton Mourao called an embassy move 'a bad idea' because of exports to Arab countries incl. an estimated $5 billion in halal food; Bolsonaro spoke of his Christian devotion to the Holy Land.

Brazil's trade office in Jerusalem was inaugurated on 15 December 2019 with Eduardo Bolsonaro and Netanyahu; Eduardo said his father would move the embassy; fears had been raised about meat exports to Arab markets.

Nigeria's Nigerian Christian Pilgrim Commission (state body) sends pilgrims to Israel and elsewhere; about 30,000 travelled Oct-Dec (2012), up from 2,000 a decade earlier; age threshold 30 for Israel to curb absconding.

entries.topic: Prophecy publishing and religious broadcasting: Lindsey, Left Behind, Robertson/CBN, pentecostal broadcast ministries, US public belief

claims.text: The Late Great Planet Earth (Zondervan, 1970; with Carole C. Carlson): 'Twenty-eight million copies had sold by 1990' (Smith 2017); described as the bestselling nonfiction book of the 1970s per the New York Times (secondary citation, Frazier 1999, Gribben 2011); film narrated by Orson Welles released January 1978; linked Matthew 24 'generation' to Israel's rebirth with a 40-year generation, read by some as 'no later than 1988'.

TheWrap obituary (30 Nov 2024): the book sold 'an estimated 35 million copies by 1999'; 'the best-selling nonfiction book of the 1970s'; it arrived three years after the June 1967 war, which Lindsey predicted would bring on the apocalypse.

Lindsey hosted International Intelligence Briefing on TBN; TBN pulled it for December 2005; Lindsey said some at the network felt his message was 'too pro- Israel and too anti- Muslim'; Paul Crouch said it was pre-empted for Christmas programming; Lindsey resigned 1 Jan 2006, returned to TBN January 2007.
Left Behind: 16 novels by Tim LaHaye and Jerry B. Jenkins, Tyndale House, 1995-2007, 'some 80 million copies' (Shelf Awareness, 2016).
Christian Post (2016): the 16-book series 'sold over 50 million copies', about 50 million by 2002; LaHaye died at 90 after a stroke, death announced 25 July 2016.
Britannica: Left Behind is a set of thriller novels 'about Evangelical Christians living through an end-times apocalypse inspired by the Book of Revelation'.
Pat Robertson launched CBN on 1 October 1961 (CBN itself says founded 1960); hosted The 700 Club 1966-2021; died 8 June 2023 aged 93.

The day after Ariel Sharon's stroke (4 Jan 2006), Robertson said on The 700 Club 'God considers this land to be his' and suggested God's opposition to a leader who divides it; Israel's tourism minister Abraham Hirchson said Robertson's help was no longer welcome for the Christian Heritage Center in the Galilee, for which Robertson led evangelicals pledging $50 million; Robertson's letter to Omri Sharon: 'I ask your forgiveness and the forgiveness of the people of Israel.'

Williams (Church History, 2015): Robertson and Hagee 'closely identified with the pentecostal-charismatic movement'; 1994 CBN Conferences event in Virginia Beach with ICEJ speakers; U.S.-based evangelists and broadcast ministries disseminated pentecostalized Christian Zionism 'well beyond North America' and helped 'catalyze a transnational, global movement'; Jonathan Cahn held meetings in India, Nigeria, Cuba, Honduras and Haiti; a 1990s study (Guth et al.) found pentecostal and charismatic leaders showed the highest political support for Israel and correlated it with premillennial eschatology.

Pew (survey July 2003, published 11 Jan 2007): 44% of Americans believe God gave the land that is now Israel to the Jewish people; 36% say Israel fulfils biblical prophecy about the Second Coming; white evangelical Protestants most likely to hold both views.
